corrected_value.authors: Damisch, L., Stoberock, B., & Mussweiler, T.
corrected_value.title: Keep your fingers crossed! How superstition improves performance.

decisions.quote:
Abstract. A recent series of experiments suggests that fostering superstitions can substantially improve performance on a variety of motor and
   cognitive tasks (Damisch, Stoberock, & Mussweiler, 2010). We conducted two high-powered and precise replications of one of these
   experiments, examining if telling participants they had a lucky golf ball could improve their performance on a 10-shot golf task relative to
   controls.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding (target 0) identify Damisch, Stoberock, and Mussweiler (2010) (doi: 10.1177/0956797610372631) as the tested original study. Both new experiments in this paper re-test Study 1 (the golf and superstition experiment) from Damisch et al. (2010), while other studies cited in the introduction and small-scale meta-analysis (Damisch, 2008; Lee et al., 2011; Aruguete et al., 2012) are discussed for background context and meta-analytic comparison rather than empirically re-tested.

decisions.quote:
We found that the effect of superstition on performance is elusive: Participants told they had a lucky ball performed almost identically
   to controls. Our failure to replicate the target study was not due to lack of impact, lack of statistical power, differences in task difficulty, nor
   differences in participant belief in luck.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding record the replication outcome for Damisch, Stoberock, and Mussweiler (2010) as 'failed'. Across both Experiment 1 (direct replication, t(122) = 0.29, p = .77, d = 0.05) and Experiment 2 (higher-impact replication, t(109) = 0.26, p = .80, d = 0.05), superstition priming failed to improve golf putting performance relative to controls (combined d = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.30]), and the authors explicitly state an overall verdict of failure to replicate the target study.

decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding classify the study as a 'replication'. The paper reports two new empirical experiments collecting new participant data (US college student samples in Experiments 1 and 2) to re-test the published golf-putting superstition finding (Study 1) of Damisch, Stoberock, and Mussweiler (2010).
